context: The box on the left reads “Open addressing: linear probing with a step size of 1.” Below it is the note “Hash function: key % 100. Keys with the same last two digits collide.”

The right side contains a single one-dimensional bucket array. Each slot holds at most one key-value pair. Between the “Index” and “Array” columns are two left braces. One groups the top 3 consecutive buckets beside the bold index 00, and the other groups the lower 5 consecutive buckets beside the bold index 76. The elements in these clusters have starting buckets 00 and 76, respectively.
description: The indices 00, 01, and 02 in the upper group and 76, 77, and 78 in the lower group are labeled. Keys 676 and 776 occupy the next two slots after 78. An ellipsis replaces their indices. Counting consecutive slots gives 79 and 80, which the table below marks as inferred. The key 076 is padded to three digits in the figure.

The starting bucket in the table comes from key % 100 and corresponds to 00 or 76 beside the brace. An element can be stored in a different bucket. Inserting the keys of each cluster into an empty table in the order shown would produce this layout, but other insertion histories could produce it as well.

frames.explanation: The two braces show how colliding elements cluster in successive slots. Trace a lookup for key 276. First compute 276 % 100 = 76. Bucket 76 contains key 076, which does not match. Bucket 77 holds 876, another mismatch. Bucket 78 holds key 276, so the lookup returns E.
frames.title: Two linear probing clusters starting at buckets 00 and 76

result: With open addressing and linear probing, an element’s actual array index can come after its starting bucket. A lookup must likewise start at key % 100 and compare keys one slot at a time.
summary: All key-value pairs are stored directly in the bucket array, with no additional linked lists. When keys collide, probe downward from the starting bucket one slot at a time and insert the pair in the first empty bucket.
